data.rationale: The crash came from tools.ts assuming company.enrich always returns a full match with every nested section present; when headcount (or the whole match) was missing, destructuring threw TypeError before the brain ever got a chance to answer, so the run crashed with no brief. The previous attempt only null-guarded fields but still let the model fabricate values/people and didn't harden against a totally missing match (matches array empty), and didn't guard search_people's profile fields either. This patch: (1) makes enrich_company fully defensive - no match returns an explicit found:false record with all nulls instead of throwing, every section read with optional chaining falling back to null; (2) makes search_people skip malformed profile entries instead of crashing, and treats next_cursor defensively; (3) wraps the tool invocation loop in agent.ts in a try/catch so any tool error becomes a step the brain can observe (enabling an explicit not-found reply) rather than crashing the whole run; (4) strengthens SYSTEM_PROMPT to explicitly instruct the model to use null for unreturned fields instead of guessing, and to only cite people/titles actually returned, directly addressing the "cites only data returned" and "no invented person" business rules without special-casing the test.

data.title: Guard enrich_company/search_people against partial data, never backfill guesses
data.rationale: The crash is in tools.ts: enrich_company destructures company.enrich's nested sections (basic_info, headcount, taxonomy, funding) and the match itself with non-null assertions (company.basic_info!.name etc.) and direct indexing (matches[0]), so a partial record missing headcount, or a response with no match at all, throws a TypeError before the brain ever sees a result, crashing the whole run (matches the neatlogs trace: 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading total)'). The previously rejected patches null-guarded fields but evidently still let the model fabricate a plausible headcount/value when it saw null, and/or didn't fully guard the no-match case and search_people's profile fields, so brief-citation violations persisted. This patch: (1) makes enrich_company fully optional-chained for every nested field and explicitly returns a `found: false`, all-null record when there is no match at all, so there is never an exception and never a fabricated fallback; (2) makes search_people skip any profile missing a name instead of crashing or inventing one, and defensively reads next_cursor; (3) wraps the tool call in agent.ts in try/catch so any residual tool error surfaces as an observable error step instead of an uncaught crash, letting the brain still produce an explicit {status:'not found'}; (4) strengthens SYSTEM_PROMPT to explicitly instruct the model that a null field (including the no-match case) must be carried through unchanged, never replaced by a guess, and that only people/titles actually returned by search_people may be listed - directly targeting the still-failing 'cites only data returned' and 'no person without a source record' rules without special-casing any specific ticket or domain.

data.title: Retry 429s honoring x-ratelimit-reset, with a time budget so the run still finishes within 5s / 8 steps
data.rationale: The previous retry attempt used fixed 100/200/400ms backoffs that are shorter than the 2s rate-limit reset window, so the retried call hit the same 429 and the agent still crashed (25/40 "no brief" failures). The fault's own hint ("x-ratelimit-reset window") tells us the server reports when the limit clears; we must wait at least that long (capped) before retrying, not guess a short backoff. We also must not blow the 5s wall-clock / 8-step budgets, so: (1) parse `HTTP 429` errors and look for a `retryAfterMs`/`x-ratelimit-reset`-style hint carried on the thrown error if the transport exposes it, defaulting to a safe ~2.1s wait that's just past the documented 2s window, (2) retry a bounded number of times (2 extra attempts) inside enrich_company and search_people, (3) keep total wait under the global 5s budget by tracking elapsed time and giving up (returning notFound rather than throwing) if a further wait would blow the deadline. This keeps the single tool call retry logic local to tools.ts (per the static-analysis finding "enrich_company never retries"), doesn't change business-rule grounding in agent.ts, and ensures the run always completes with a brief or explicit not-found instead of crashing, honoring the 5s/8-step/5-credit constraints: company.enrich is still called at most 3 times (6 credits risk) — to stay within the 5-credit budget, we only retry once (not twice) for enrich_company, which keeps worst case at 2 calls × 2 credits = 4 credits, safely under 5.

data.rationale: tools.ts only retries 429 rate-limit errors. A transient 500 from /person/search (and potentially /company/enrich) is thrown straight through withRateLimitRetry's isRateLimited check, which returns false for 5xx, so the error propagates and crashes the run (20/20 crashed trials, "run crashed, no brief"). The fix generalizes the transient-error detection to also recognize 5xx server errors (HTTP 500-599) and retries them with a short fixed backoff (not the rate-limit reset wait, since there's no reset header for a 500), still respecting the overall wall-clock budget. On exhausting retries for a 5xx, enrich_company treats it as "not found" and search_people returns whatever people were already collected, exactly like the existing 429 handling, so the run always completes with a grounded brief or explicit not-found instead of crashing.

data.title: Add per-call timeout to Crustdata transport calls so a slow enrich/search can't hang the run
data.rationale:
The static analysis correctly identifies the root cause: enrich_company (and search_people) call transport() with no timeout. When company.enrich takes 10s to respond, the awaited promise never resolves within the run's 5s budget, so the run hangs past the deadline instead of failing fast and falling back to "not found"/partial results. The retry/backoff logic already budgets wall-clock time correctly for 429/5xx, but it has no way to bound an individual call that simply never returns (or returns very late) — there's no race against a timeout.

The fix wraps every transport() call in a timeout that's capped by the remaining run budget (minus safety margin). If the call doesn't settle in time, it rejects with a distinguishable timeout error, which the existing isTransient-like handling treats as a soft failure: enrich_company returns {notFound:true, domain} and search_people returns whatever people it already collected. This keeps the run within the 5s wall-clock limit and guarantees the agent still produces a grounded brief or "not found" instead of hanging, without changing any business-rule semantics (no credits are over-charged, no invented people/data, retries for 429/5xx remain unaffected since a slow-but-eventually-erroring call will now time out instead of hanging the whole process).

data.title: Person search body is cut off mid-JSON
data.hypothesis: If a /person/search response is truncated, ResearchBot crashes because it parses the body without validating or retrying.

data.title: Treat unparseable (truncated) person-search JSON as a transient failure
data.rationale:
Root cause: search_people's pagination loop does `JSON.parse(raw)` on the person.search response body with no error handling. A truncated body throws a SyntaxError that is not an Error our isTransient() check recognizes (it only looks for HTTP 429/5xx/timeout message patterns), so the catch block's `if (!isTransient(err)) throw err;` re-throws it, and the uncaught SyntaxError propagates out of runResearchBot and crashes the run. That matches the evidence exactly: "SyntaxError: Expected ':' after property name in JSON" killing the run after 2 steps.

The fix treats a malformed/truncated JSON body from person.search the same way the code already treats a transient HTTP fault: catch the parse error for the current page, stop paginating, and return whatever leader profiles were already collected from prior pages (or an empty list if this was the first page) rather than crash. This mirrors the existing resilience pattern used for 429/5xx/timeout (collect-what-we-have-and-move-on) instead of inventing new behavior, keeps groundBrief's "only cite what a tool actually returned" guarantee intact (we never fabricate people or titles - we only stop reading a corrupted page), and still lets the run finish with a brief or an explicit not-found rather than hang or crash. enrich_company's parseCompany is unaffected since the fault/evidence is specific to person.search; no change was needed there.

I did not change retry/backoff semantics, credit budgets, or the grounding logic in agent.ts, since those already correctly handle "fewer people than hoped" and "no company found" cases - the only gap was the unguarded JSON.parse on a truncated person-search body.

data.title: Person search cursor never advances
data.hypothesis: If /person/search ignores the cursor and keeps returning page 1 with a next_cursor, ResearchBot pages forever: unbounded calls, credits and time.

data.title: Cap pagination pages, cursor progress, and overall step/call budgets
data.rationale:
search_people's pagination loop trusted next_cursor unconditionally: if the API returns the same page/cursor forever (or a cursor that never advances), the loop runs until the process-level wall-clock deadline fires a TimeoutError deep inside a single call, after already issuing thousands of requests and burning thousands of credits/calls before that error is even thrown. That blows the 5s/5-credit/20-calls-per-endpoint/8-steps budgets long before the timeout mechanism can stop it, because the timeout only guards one in-flight transport call, not the number of iterations of the do/while loop around it.

Fix at the root: bound the pagination loop itself by a small, generous-but-finite max page count, and detect a non-advancing cursor (the actual fault here: cursor ignored, same page echoed back with a next_cursor) by comparing the new cursor to the previous one and stopping as soon as it repeats or the page returned no new profiles. This makes a single search_people call cost at most a handful of API calls/credits regardless of a stuck backend, independent of and in addition to the per-call timeout. Also add a hard step cap in the agent loop as defense in depth so a brain stuck deciding to call tools forever cannot run away either, surfacing a "not found" instead of hanging past the step/time budget.
